transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-25
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Patel (SummitPay CTO), Sofia Ramirez (SummitPay ML Eng), Noah Clarke (SummitPay Platform), Ava Liu (SummitPay Security)

00:00 - Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, im maya from redwood, im the ae on the account, with liam and priya on the se side, hows everyone doing
00:12 - Jordan Patel: good thanks, busy quarter, appreciate you fitting this in
00:16 - Maya Chen: quick agenda, we want to walk through optimize: batching and prefix / kv cache levers, show the cost model with your baseline numbers, and propose a pilot to validate savings, any other items to add?
00:28 - Noah Clarke: security question later but, otherwise that sounds good
00:32 - Liam Ortega: great, i can jump into the technical tradeoffs - i'll start with batching basics, then prefix and kv cache examples
00:40 - Liam Ortega: so starting with batching - the idea is we aggregate concurrent requests into a batch to amortize per-call overhead, which reduces p99 token cost when throughput allows it, but it can add tail latency if you wait too long for batch fill
01:05 - Sofia Ramirez: how much does batching help for small prompts, like our payment verification flow? those are usually 30 to 50 tokens, high qps bursts during peak minutes
01:14 - Liam Ortega: good question. for short sequences batching often gives linear improvements until the model compute saturates. with 32-token requests, moving from batch size 1 -> 8 can give 3x throughput improvement on gpus we commonly use; exact numbers depend on model (quantized vs fp16)
01:30 - Priya Singh: and practically we set a max latency target, e.g. p95 250ms; the runtime uses a hybrid batcher that has a max wait (e.g. 20-40ms) and a max batch size. for SummitPay i'd suggest target batch wait of 25ms and observe p95 impact in pilot
01:48 - Jordan Patel: okay, but our SLO for payment verification is 200ms p95, so we need tight tail behavior. if batching risks missing that during bursts it's a hard no
01:58 - Liam Ortega: understood - that's why we profile with your traffic shape. batching config is workload-aware; you can also route critical endpoints to a low-latency pool (dedicated) and route non-critical to a cost-optimized pool.
02:10 - Sofia Ramirez: can you explain prefix cache vs kv cache? we have a lot of repeated prefixes in our user flows
02:20 - Liam Ortega: sure - prefix cache stores the encoder/kv states for common prefixes so the model doesn't recompute initial tokens; it's great when you have repeating system prompts or long structured prompts. KV cache is per-conversation key/value cache for autoregressive decoding - we often call it the prefix / kv cache feature; the naming is a bit messy across vendors
02:40 - Maya Chen: (laughs) yep vendor naming is always fun; the important part is the effect: less compute per request for repeated prefixes, meaning lower per-token cost and lower GPU time
02:50 - Noah Clarke: what about memory - if we cache lots of prefixes, gpu memory could blow up, right?
:02:56 - Liam Ortega: memory is the limiter - for long seq lengths prefix entries can be large. our runtime supports TTLs and LRU eviction and also profiling to surface the hit rate vs memory tradeoff. typical approach: pick top 200 prefixes, set TTL 24h, monitor hit rate, then expand as needed.
03:16 - Sofia Ramirez: so for our use case, which is lots of structured prompts but not super long, prefix cache sounds promising
03:24 - Priya Singh: we also recommend a hybrid: prefix caching for the stable base prompt + kv cache for ongoing session states. that gives best of both worlds
03:34 - Jordan Patel: show us the cost model - how much can we expect to save?
03:38 - Maya Chen: we prepared a cost model with your rough numbers - avg qps 1200 during peak, average tokens per request 42, retention windows etc - i'll share the sheet after, but high level: with moderate batching + prefix caching we estimate 40-55% gross token compute cost reduction for the high-volume endpoint
03:58 - Sofia Ramirez: 40-55% is huge, does that include extra infra cost for cache memory / larger nodes?
04:06 - Liam Ortega: yes, sheet treats cache memory as a delta of instance class. so costs are net savings: saved GPU cycles minus marginal VM / GPU memory cost. for example moving to 2x memory instances might add 15% infra cost but reduce token compute by 50%, so net about 35% savings
04:26 - Noah Clarke: show numbers please - can you paste a sample row?
04:30 - Maya Chen: sure - (links) shared: https://drive.google.com/summitpay-redwood-cost-model (shared sheet) - row example: baseline tokens/month 1.9B, baseline GPU hours 1200, baseline infra $X, optimized GPU hours 520, optimized infra $Y, net monthly savings ~35%
04:52 - Ava Liu: on security - will any customer data be stored in the cache? we need encryption at rest and auditability
04:58 - Priya Singh: good question. cache entries are stored encrypted at rest when using Private or Dedicated with KMS. in Hosted we also encrypt at rest and offer options to use bring-your-own-key for customers on the enterprise plan. audit logs include cache hit/miss traces for debugging; we can redact payloads for compliance
05:22 - Ava Liu: do you persist full prompts in logs? PCI implications if those include payment tokens
05:28 - Maya Chen: no; by default we dont log full prompt content for sensitive endpoints. we support redaction rules and token scrubbing. we'll include our security pack with examples of redaction configs
05:38 - Jordan Patel: back to pilot - what would success criteria look like?
05:41 - Liam Ortega: a) measure hit rate (target >=45% after warmup) for top prefixes, b) net token compute reduction >=30% within 2 weeks, c) p95 latency within your 200ms SLO for critical route. those are measurable via Console dashboards and the shared sheet
06:00 - Sofia Ramirez: how do you handle model variants fallback? if cached prefix was generated by one model version and we roll to a new one?
06:09 - Priya Singh: we key the cache by model version and prompt fingerprint. during rollouts we can keep the cache separate per-version or have an automatic invalidation policy. we recommend canarying and keeping cache warming steps in rollout plan
06:22 - Noah Clarke: what's the impact on cold-starts - if cache misses spike during release we might see burst compute costs
06:28 - Liam Ortega: true - we recommend staged warms: pre-warm top prefixes into cache before traffic switches, and during pilot we simulate release to quantify cold start cost
06:40 - Jordan Patel: whats the engineering effort on our side to integrate? we want minimal changes to code path
06:45 - Maya Chen: for hosted API, minimal - you pass a cache key header or use the prompt fingerprinting helper from our SDK. for Private/Dedicated there's an optional sidecar library but still minimal: 1-2 endpoints to instrument and a small config file for TTLs and policies
06:59 - Sofia Ramirez: you mentioned SDK helpers - do you expose batching hints at the client level or is it purely server-side?
07:06 - Liam Ortega: batching is server-side. SDKs provide connection pooling and optional request grouping helpers (useful for serverless or per-request containers). you dont have to change your prompt logic to get batching benefits
07:18 - Jordan Patel: ok, show me a real pilot config - instance types, batch targets, TTL, monitoring hooks
07:24 - Liam Ortega: (shares screen) proposed pilot: - Dedicated small pool of 2 x a10x GPUs (or v100 equivalent) with 256GB mem for cache - batch target 8, max wait 25ms - prefix cache top 250 prefixes, TTL 24h - instrumentation: per-endpoint token counter, cache hit/miss, p95/p99 latency - expected baseline vs pilot monthly delta in the shared sheet
07:58 - Noah Clarke: are those instance choices negotiable? massaging instance types helps with our cloud discounts
08:03 - Priya Singh: absolutely - we can map to your preferred instance families and show delta in cost model; a10x was just an example
08:12 - Sofia Ramirez: any gotchas with quantized models? some of our internal benchmarks used int8 and saw different perf characteristics
08:20 - Liam Ortega: quantization changes kernel selection and memory tradeoffs. sometimes int8 reduces compute but increases memory for activation caching; our runtime has tuning knobs and we'll include model-specific guidance in the pilot plan. we typically run small microbenchmarks to pick optimal quantization & batch targets before scaling
08:39 - Jordan Patel: what's the expected timeline to get measurable results in the pilot? 2 weeks enough?
08:43 - Liam Ortega: yes - 2 weeks with warmup (2-3 days) usually enough to reach stable hit rates and see steady-state savings
08:49 - Maya Chen: action items recap: we'll send the tailored cost model, security pack, and pilot config; liam will scope the pilot infra and runbook; you'll provide traffic samples and confirm stakeholders. does that align?
08:59 - Jordan Patel: yes, i'll loop in product and infra; sofia will share sample traffic logs and top 500 prompts
09:06 - Sofia Ramirez: yes i'll export that by friday
09:09 - Noah Clarke: one more question - can you show how Console dashboards look for cache metrics?
09:13 - Liam Ortega: quick demo: (switches to Console) per-route dashboard shows token breakdown, cache hit rate, prefix heatmap, and per-batch size histogram. you can set alerts on hit rate drop or p95 regressions.
09:31 - Ava Liu: will alerts include audit information for security incidents?
09:35 - Priya Singh: alerts integrate with your pager and we can include sanitized traces for forensic triage. raw prompt text stays redacted unless you explicitly enable full debug in a secure, audited workflow
09:48 - Jordan Patel: ok that helps. pricing question: how do you bill for cache resources or saved tokens?
09:54 - Maya Chen: hosted is primarily token + infra units; we show token savings in the invoice credits model when pilot results are accepted into production. for Dedicated we price reserved capacity and for cache memory we include it in the instance SKU; we can model both approaches in the spreadsheet
10:10 - Sofia Ramirez: and during the pilot we can get temporary credits?
10:14 - Maya Chen: yes often we offer pilot credits to offset initial infra cost - we'll put that number in the sheet for transparency
10:20 - Jordan Patel: any references or case studies?
10:23 - Maya Chen: we have a short case study (links) "Atlas Financial" where they got ~42% token compute reduction with prefix caching + batching; i'll attach it in follow-up
10:33 - Noah Clarke: cool. last operational question - how do we rollback if the cache causes unexpected regressions?
10:38 - Liam Ortega: rollout policies include automatic fallback: we can disable cache or pin routing to baseline model instantly, and Console supports immediate disable of cache layer with a single toggle.
10:49 - Sofia Ramirez: ok that's reassuring
10:51 - Maya Chen: any final questions?
10:53 - Jordan Patel: none from me, thanks for the clear plan
10:55 - Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll send materials and schedule pilot kickoff, talk soon
11:00 - (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: some speaker labels may be slightly off and timestamps are approximate. Links referenced: cost model sheet (drive), Atlas Financial case study (pdf), security pack (shared link).
